title: Vibrations and waves
summary: Types of waves, reflection, interference, sound and electromagnetic waves.
cards.0.p: A vibration that travels through a medium is called a mechanical wave, and a wave carries energy. If the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel, the wave is transverse. A wave on a rope is an example. If the vibration is parallel to the direction of travel, the wave is longitudinal. Sound is an example.
cards.0.key: Light is a transverse wave too, but it is not mechanical. Light needs no medium and travels through a vacuum.
cards.1.p: The distance between two neighboring crests is the wavelength (λ). The height from equilibrium to a crest is the amplitude (A), and the number of waves per second is the frequency. The speed of the wave is v = λ·f.
cards.1.svg#5: f: number of waves per second (Hz)
cards.1.key: The period is T = 1/f. The amplitude sets the energy. When the amplitude doubles, the energy becomes 4 times larger.
cards.1.etk.soru: Change the wavelength and the frequency: v = λ·f.
cards.2.h: Speed depends on the medium, frequency on the source
cards.2.p: The medium sets the speed of a wave. A wave travels fast on a tight rope and slowly on a thick rope. The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change, but λ does.
cards.2.svg#7: v = λ·f: with f constant, v and λ change by the same ratio
cards.2.key: On a stretched rope v = √(F/μ). F is the force stretching the rope, and μ is the mass per unit length of the rope.
cards.3.h: Reflection of a pulse on a spring
cards.3.p: A pulse reflected from a fixed end tied to a wall comes back inverted. So a crest returns as a trough. From a free end, a ring sliding on a rod, the pulse reflects upright. The transmitted pulse always stays upright.
cards.3.key: Going from thin to thick, the reflected pulse comes back inverted. Going from thick to thin, it comes back upright.
cards.4.p: When two waves overlap at the same point, their displacements add. This is called interference. A crest meeting a crest gives constructive interference, and a crest meeting an equal trough gives destructive interference. The waves then continue on their way unchanged.
cards.4.key: In destructive interference the energy does not disappear. When the waves separate, both return to their original shape.
cards.5.p: Two identical waves traveling in opposite directions on the same rope form a standing wave. The points that never vibrate are nodes, and the points that vibrate with the largest amplitude are antinodes.
cards.5.svg#4: node: never vibrates · antinode: vibrates most
cards.5.key: The distance between two neighboring nodes or two neighboring antinodes is λ/2.
cards.5.once.soru: Both ends of a guitar string are fixed. Do these ends vibrate when the string is played?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fixed ends cannot move. So in a standing wave these ends are always nodes.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The points that vibrate most are antinodes, and they are in the middle of the string.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Tied ends do not vibrate at all.
cards.6.p: For a wave hitting a straight barrier, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The angles are measured from the line perpendicular to the barrier, called the normal. A straight wave reflected from a parabolic barrier gathers at the focus.
cards.6.svg#7: the wave gathers at the focus
cards.6.key: A ripple tank is a shallow, glass-bottomed tray for watching water waves. A circular wave leaving the focus reflects from the parabola as a straight wave.
cards.6.once.soru: A water wave reaches a straight wall at 30° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: 60° is the angle with the wall. Angles are measured from the normal.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. 90° would not make sense here, since the wave arrives at 30°.
cards.7.h: Water waves: from deep to shallow
cards.7.p: Water waves slow down in a shallow region. The frequency does not change, and the wavelength gets shorter. A wave that meets the boundary at an angle is refracted. Going from deep to shallow, the wave bends toward the normal.
cards.7.key: A wave going from shallow to deep bends away from the normal.
cards.7.once.soru: Why do ocean waves turn parallel to the shore even when they approach at an angle?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.yazi: They slow down in the shallows
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The part of the wave nearer the shore slows down first. So the wave front turns and becomes parallel to the shore.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Waves turn near the shore even with no wind.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: The turning happens in shallow water, before the wave reaches the shore.
cards.8.p: A wave passing through a narrow gap bends into the region behind the barrier. This is called diffraction. Diffraction is noticeable when the gap is close to the wavelength or smaller. Two identical sources produce interference lines.
cards.8.key: In diffraction λ, f and the speed do not change. With light, the same effect gives bright and dark fringes in the double-slit experiment.
cards.8.once.soru: You can hear someone behind a door but you cannot see them. Why?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The wavelength of sound is close to the size of the doorway, so sound bends around the corner. The wavelength of light is very small.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Light is much faster than sound.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Sound does not come through the wall either. It bends through the opening.
cards.9.p: Sound is a longitudinal, mechanical wave that compresses and thins out the air. So it does not travel through a vacuum. The speed of sound is greatest in solids and smallest in gases. In air it is about 343 m/s.
cards.9.key: Sound travels at about 1480 m/s in water. The human ear hears sounds between 20 and 20 000 Hz. Sounds below this range are called infrasound, and those above it ultrasound.
cards.9.once.soru: Can we hear the sound of an explosion in space from Earth?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Sound needs matter to travel. So it cannot travel through the vacuum of space.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Sound does not travel through a vacuum at all.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: We see the light, but we do not hear the sound.
cards.10.p: The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency. Its intensity grows with amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB). Timbre is the wave shape that lets you tell a violin from a piano.
cards.10.key: Every +10 dB means the intensity is 10 times larger. So a 70 dB sound has 10 times the intensity of a 60 dB sound.
cards.10.once.soru: Why does the same note sound different on a violin and on a piano?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The frequency is the same, but the wave shapes are different.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: The same note has the same frequency.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The air sets the speed of sound, not the source.
cards.11.p: You hear a higher pitch when a sound source approaches and a lower pitch when it moves away. This is called the Doppler effect. The wavelength is shorter in front of the source and longer behind it. The source's own frequency does not change.
cards.11.key: The speed of sound in air does not change either. Speed radar and Doppler ultrasound use this effect.
cards.11.once.soru: An ambulance with its siren on passes you and moves away. How does the sound change?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Behind it the wavelength is longer, so the frequency you hear drops.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: The pitch rises while the source is approaching.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: The source is moving, so the frequency you hear changes.
cards.12.p: Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves. They are transverse waves and need no medium. Their speed in a vacuum is c = 3×108 m/s. As the frequency increases, the wavelength gets shorter and the energy increases.
cards.12.svg#7: frequency and energy rise, λ shrinks
cards.12.svg#8: in a vacuum all travel at c = 3×10⁸ m/s
cards.12.key: The order is radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma. In visible light, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.
cards.12.etk.soru: Put the electromagnetic waves in order from shortest to longest wavelength. Hint: as the frequency increases, the wavelength gets shorter.
cards.12.once.soru: How does sunlight cross empty space and reach the Earth?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: An electromagnetic wave travels through a vacuum too.
cards.13.p: Ultrasound images a baby, and sonar measures depth. These are mechanical waves. Radio and phones carry communication, a microwave oven heats food, and X-rays show bones. These are electromagnetic waves.
cards.13.key: A mechanical wave needs a medium, while an electromagnetic wave also travels through a vacuum. A seismograph records earthquake waves, and radar finds aircraft.
cards.13.once.soru: Which kind of wave carries a phone call through a satellite?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Only an electromagnetic wave can cross the vacuum of space.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: Sound does not travel through a vacuum.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave too, and it needs a medium.
cards.14.p:
• A wave carries energy and is transverse or longitudinal.
• v = λ·f. The speed depends on the medium, and the frequency on the source.
• A pulse reflects inverted from a fixed end and upright from a free end.
• Sound is longitudinal and does not travel through a vacuum.
• The speed of EM waves in a vacuum is c = 3×108 m/s.
quiz.0.q: A source produces 5 waves per second, and the distance between two neighboring crests is 0.4 m. What is the speed of the wave in m/s?
quiz.1.q: A sound wave passes from air into water. How do its frequency, speed and wavelength change?
quiz.1.o.0: Frequency stays the same. Speed and wavelength increase
quiz.1.o.1: Frequency stays the same. Speed and wavelength decrease
quiz.1.o.2: Frequency increases. Speed and wavelength stay the same
quiz.1.e: The source sets the frequency, and it does not change. Sound is faster in water (about 1480 m/s) than in air (about 343 m/s). Since v = λ·f, the wavelength increases by the same ratio.
quiz.1.y.1: You assumed that what happens on a thick rope is true for sound as well. Sound is about 4 times faster in water than in air.
quiz.1.y.2: The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change.
quiz.1.y.3: The medium sets the speed. Water is a different medium, so the speed changes.
quiz.2.q: A pulse (a crest) travels along a spring. In each case, how does it come back or pass through? Inverted (a trough) or upright (a crest)?
quiz.2.ogeler.2.0: Reflected going from a thin to a thick spring
quiz.2.ogeler.3.0: Reflected going from a thick to a thin spring
quiz.2.ogeler.4.0: Transmitted from a thin to a thick spring
quiz.2.ogeler.5.0: Transmitted from a thick to a thin spring
quiz.2.e: A fixed end and a thick spring reflect the pulse inverted. A free end and a thin spring reflect it upright. The pulse transmitted between two springs stays upright in every case.
quiz.3.q: When an ambulance with its siren on approaches you, you hear a higher pitch. What is the reason?
quiz.3.o.0: The frequency the siren produces increases
quiz.3.o.1: The speed of sound in air increases
quiz.3.o.2: The wave crests reach your ear closer together
quiz.3.o.3: The amplitude of the sound increases
quiz.3.e: In the Doppler effect, the source's own frequency and the speed of sound do not change. In front of an approaching source the wavelength is shorter, and you perceive a higher frequency.
quiz.3.y.0: The frequency the siren itself produces does not change. What changes is how often the waves reach your ear.
quiz.3.y.1: The speed of sound depends on the medium and does not change with the motion of the source. What changes is the wavelength.
quiz.3.y.3: Amplitude sets the intensity of the sound. A higher pitch comes from a higher frequency.
A:ozet: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves, set the wavelength with v = λ·f, send a wave into another medium, see what amplitude does, reflect a pulse and make waves interfere.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Send a wave first along a rope, then along a spring, and watch the red particles.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Does the red particle travel along with the wave?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Look at the dashed line. The particle stays around the place where it started.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A wave carries energy, not matter. When you throw a stone into water the rings move outward, but a floating leaf just bobs up and down in place.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In a longitudinal wave too, the particle moves back and forth and returns to the same place.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The speed of a wave is v = λ · f. The wave will now pass from a thin rope to a thick rope.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: What changes on the thick rope?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Speed and λ decrease, f is the same
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The wave slows down on the thick rope. The frequency does not change, so by v = λ·f the wavelength gets shorter too.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: f decreases, λ is the same
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: On the thick rope the waves bunch up and the front slows down.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Amplitude is the height from equilibrium to a crest. The two ropes are identical. The upper wave has amplitude A, and the lower one 3A.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy, but it does not travel faster.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A small amplitude does not speed a wave up. Both waves are in the same medium.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The two waves travel at the same speed on identical ropes. The medium sets the speed, not the amplitude.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The source shakes the rope, and the wave travels to the right. The triangle follows a crest, and the red dot is a piece of the rope. Change the frequency, the wave speed (the tension in the rope) and the amplitude. Find the following for yourself.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: With the speed at 4 m/s, raise the frequency from 1 Hz to 2 Hz. What happens to the wavelength?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: λ dropped from 4 m to 2 m. On the same rope the speed does not change. So when the frequency doubles, the wavelength is cut in half: v = λ·f.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Set the frequency to 4 Hz but keep the wavelength at 2 m.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: For the wavelength to stay the same, the speed had to double as well, so you tightened the rope. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: Bring the wavelength down to 0.5 m and watch the red dot.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: At a speed of 2 m/s and a frequency of 4 Hz, λ = 0.5 m. While the wave traveled to the right, the red dot only vibrated up and down. So a wave carries energy, not matter.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A single disturbance on a spring is called a pulse. Send the pulse first to a fixed end tied to a wall, then to a free end with a ring sliding on a rod.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: At which end does the pulse come back inverted?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: At the free end the ring rises with the pulse, and the pulse comes back as a crest.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The pulse pulls the wall up, and the wall pulls the rope down. This is an action-reaction pair. So the crest comes back as a trough.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In the trial with the free end, the pulse came back as a crest.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Two pulses are heading toward each other. When they meet at the same point, their displacements add. Make the rope look flat at the moment they meet.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: When a crest met an equal trough, the displacements canceled each other. This is called destructive interference.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: To cancel a crest you need an equal trough.
A:kapanis.0: A wave carries energy, not matter. The particles of the medium vibrate in place.
A:kapanis.1: In a transverse wave the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel, and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Sound is a longitudinal wave.
A:kapanis.2: The speed of a wave is v = λ·f. The medium sets the speed, and the source sets the frequency. Amplitude changes the energy, not the speed.
A:kapanis.3: A pulse reflects inverted from a fixed end and upright from a free end. When waves meet, their displacements add.
A:kapanis.4: Pushes at the natural frequency make the amplitude grow. This is called resonance.
